groups.text: A busy server holds thousands of open connections, and most of them are quiet at any moment.
A thread for each one would park thousands of threads, at about a megabyte of memory each.
Jetty splits the work into three jobs, and every thread comes from one pool: a QueuedThreadPool, with at least eight threads and at most two hundred.
The connector leases a few of them for good.
One becomes the acceptor.
It calls accept, and hands each new socket on.
On four C P Us, two more become selectors.
Each one runs a select loop, E poll on Linux, and watches many sockets at once for readiness: up to thousands each.
The pool also keeps a few idle threads ready, called reserved threads.
And on the right sits your handler.
Follow one request.
A client connects.
The acceptor accepts the socket, and hands it to a selector.
The client sends its request.
The selector sees that socket is readable, and makes a task: parse the request, and call your handler.
Your handler is declared blocking.
Which thread runs that task?
Usually, the selector thread itself.
First a reserved thread takes over the watching.
Then the selector thread runs your handler, while the request is still warm in its C P U cache.
Jetty calls this Execute-Produce-Consume.
With no reserved thread free, the task goes into the pool's queue, and a pool thread picks it up.
That is Produce-Execute-Consume: a hand-off and cold caches, but no stall.
A handler that declares itself non-blocking skips the hand-off.
The selector thread runs it on the spot, just like a Netty event loop.
That is Produce-Consume.
But that is a promise.
Break it with a JDBC call, and every other socket on that selector waits behind your query.
The promise is your handler's superclass.
Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking says: I never block.
Handler.Abstract says: I may block.
Use it for anything that waits.
The rule: acceptors take connections, selectors notice ready sockets, and Jetty picks who runs your handler from what it declares.
So declare it honestly.
A quick check.
Set the reserved threads to zero, and call a blocking handler.
Which thread runs it?
